post1.text:
Most executives believe leadership gets easier as a company scales. It does not. It gets more dangerous.

When a business crosses the $50M threshold, the leadership instincts that got it there often become the exact liabilities that stall the next phase. Speed of decision-making, personal relationships with every key player, and founder-level intensity simply do not transfer at scale without deliberate redesign.

Recent reporting on executives who successfully scale companies points to one consistent pattern: the leaders who win at this stage are the ones who actively rewire how they operate, not just how they hire.

Here is what that actually looks like in practice:

First, your communication cadence must evolve before your org chart does. Second, accountability systems need to outlive your personal oversight. Third, the leaders below you must be developed to make decisions you once owned.

Scaling is not a growth problem. It is a leadership architecture problem.

What is the one leadership behavior you know you need to change as your company grows, but have not changed yet?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Yahoo Finance draws a compelling parallel between Scale Smart Leaders and Jeff Bezos on how executives should be developed inside growing organizations.

The connection is not coincidental. At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies moving through the $50M to $500M range. The executives who scale the company are rarely the ones who were simply promoted. They are the ones who were intentionally built.

That distinction matters. If your organization does not have a deliberate process for developing the leaders two levels below you, you are building a ceiling into your own growth model without realizing it.

Leadership development at scale is not an HR initiative. It is a business strategy.

post3.text:
Recent coverage of executives who successfully scale organizations keeps circling back to one uncomfortable truth: the leader has to change, not just the company.

That is exactly where Katherine Slain starts in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

The chapter is titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, and the title is not hyperbole. Katherine makes the case that at this stage of growth, weak leadership does not just slow a company down. It puts the entire organization at risk in ways most founders do not see coming until it is too late.

One insight she surfaces early: the leadership identity that built your company to $50M is a starting point, not a finish line. What you do with that identity next determines everything.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Scaling a business past $50M is not primarily a capital problem or a talent problem. It is a leadership problem. The habits, instincts, and decision-making patterns that built the company become structural risks at the next level. What separates companies that break through from those that plateau almost always traces back to whether the leader at the top was willing to change first.

post1.text:
Most business owners think their multiple is determined at the closing table. It isn't. It's determined years before you ever talk to a buyer.

Recent data from the advisory M&A market confirms what we see with clients every day: larger, better-organized firms are commanding significantly higher multiples and attracting more sophisticated deal structures. Size matters, but so does how you've built what you own.

Three things that move your multiple before you go to market:

1. Intangible assets are chronically undervalued because owners can't articulate them clearly. If you can't explain the value, neither can a buyer.

2. EBITDA quality beats EBITDA size. Buyers pay more for earnings they trust than for earnings they have to verify three times.

3. Customer concentration is a silent multiple-killer. One client representing 30% of revenue is a risk flag, not a bragging right.

You don't get a second chance to build the business a buyer wants to own.

What's the one thing in your business right now that you know would concern a serious acquirer?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey explored how strategic buyers consistently outperform financial investors in M&A when they build a repeatable capability for identifying and capturing synergies rather than treating each deal as a one-off event.

This matters enormously if you are on the sell side.

When a strategic buyer comes to the table, they are not just buying your earnings. They are buying what your business adds to theirs. If you understand that before negotiations begin, you can position your company to command a premium instead of accepting a standard market multiple.

At Autobahn, we work with $50M+ companies to help leadership teams see their business the way an acquirer does, long before a deal is in play. That perspective changes how you build, not just how you sell.

Read the McKinsey piece here and think about which type of buyer your business is most valuable to: https://news.google.

post3.text:
Larger firms are getting higher multiples. That trend in the advisory M&A market is not luck. It's the result of intentional preparation.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond, tackles exactly this. The chapter is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two people who have sat on both sides of the deal table.

One thing they make clear: your multiple is not a reward for hard work. It's a reflection of how well you've removed risk and created certainty for a buyer. Most owners find out too late that those are two very different things to build toward.

There is a framework in this chapter that changes how you think about growth decisions today, not just at exit.

post1.text:
Most leadership teams don't have a strategy problem. They have a reality problem.

They confuse having a plan with executing one. Bain research confirms it: the gap between strategy and execution isn't a planning failure. It's a prioritization failure. Too many initiatives, too little accountability, and no honest conversation about what actually gets done when things get hard.

Here's what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They treat the annual offsite as the strategy. Real strategy lives in the weekly decisions your managers make without you in the room.

2. They measure outputs, not progress. Revenue is a lagging indicator. What are your leading indicators telling you right now?

3. They over-index on alignment at the top and under-invest in execution at the middle. Your VP layer is where strategy goes to die or thrive.

If you are running a $50M+ company, your bottleneck is almost never the idea. It is the system that is supposed to deliver it.

What is the one strategic priority at your company that everyone agrees on but nobody is actually moving forward?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Harvard Business School Online tackles one of the most persistent problems in growing companies: getting employees to actually believe in and act on strategic initiatives.

The article is right. Buy-in is not a communication problem. It is a design problem.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies scaling past $50M. Leadership announces a strategy. Managers nod. Nothing changes. Why? Because employees were handed a destination, not a reason to move.

The fix is not a better slide deck. It is earlier involvement, clearer connection between individual roles and company outcomes, and leaders who are willing to hear real friction before it becomes real failure.

If your team is not moving on what matters most, start by asking who was in the room when you built the plan.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiXEFVX3lxTE10NVhQek5OWEJXOHdQLW1iZFF5dWN0Vy1TS0VJMzJUYmQ1ZWRVUzZLWk50QTdNbHpEd3JtS2ZfbFFZSWR6MTNJMnZraWMzUVNrUVl6LTE5T2FCMVhW?oc=5

post3.text:
Strategic planning looks very different when you have actually sold fish food and Nike shoes for a living.

Chapter 3 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes.' Authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall bring hard-won, ground-level perspective to the question every scaling company eventually faces: why does a plan that looks brilliant in the boardroom fall apart in the field?

Their answer has nothing to do with frameworks. It has everything to do with what people actually do when no one is watching.

The insight they share in this chapter reframes how $50M-plus leaders should think about the relationship between strategy and the humans responsible for executing it.

It is not what you expect.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Your strategy did not fail because it was a bad strategy. It failed because the people responsible for executing it were never truly part of building it. Companies scaling from $50M to $500M consistently hit the same wall: leadership thinks in plans, the organization lives in habits. Closing that gap is not a planning exercise. It is a cultural and operational discipline that most leadership teams have never been taught.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M+ don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit. There's a difference, and it's costing them more than they realize.

A habit is what your team does by default. A strategy is a deliberate system built to scale. When G2 recently reviewed the state of sales training and onboarding tools for 2026, the underlying message was clear: companies are investing in software before they've defined the process the software is supposed to support. That's backwards.

Here's what actually matters at your stage:

1. Your sales motion must be documented and repeatable before you hire your next rep. Otherwise you're scaling chaos.

2. Quota attainment means nothing if you can't explain why your top performers win. Pattern recognition is a strategy. Gut feel is not.

3. The gap between your best and worst seller is a strategy problem, not a talent problem.

Every quarter you operate without a defined sales strategy is a quarter you're leaving growth on the table.

What's the one part of your sales process you'd be embarrassed to put in writing?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Built In profiled Lindsey Schidlovsky's sales leadership career at Toast, and it's worth a read for any executive building or rebuilding a sales organization.

What stood out to us at Autobahn: the throughline of her career wasn't just hitting numbers. It was building repeatable systems inside a company that was scaling fast.

That's exactly what separates companies that grow from $50M to $100M from the ones that stall. The leaders who scale aren't necessarily the best closers. They're the ones who can install a sales culture, define the right motion, and develop the team to execute it consistently.

If you're running a growth-stage company and your sales strategy still lives in your top rep's head, that's your biggest risk.

Read the full article here and think about what a sales leadership infrastructure looks like in your business: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikgFBVV95cUxPdGpoMWpySkdrLXE5ZDNvZk52REVxa2dhZml3RUF2WmZ2X296OUkwTktYb2xCYU9MQW1WUzYxWTRrQ2gzY3lqQ2dlSHduSFJwU1AyX1BBVF9xOVNtQkhVUU9UbEtlektsN0YtMXVGRy1vSlZZVUJydWNOOUdhc2VKaVRiRjZ1ejJHVzVuclpQWnhFUQ?oc=5

post3.text:
G2's recent roundup of sales training and onboarding tools for 2026 highlights something we see constantly in scaling companies: leaders invest in tools hoping the tools will create clarity. They rarely do.

Chapter 4 of our upcoming book, 'Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond,' tackles this head on. The chapter is titled 'Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation,' and it's authored by Deb and Brandon.

Their core argument is direct: without a defined sales strategy, every dollar you spend on headcount, technology, or training is partially wasted. You are essentially donating margin to the market.

The chapter gives leaders a framework for building a sales strategy that actually scales, not one that depends on your best rep showing up.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your color palette. It is not your tagline. Your brand is what people say about you when you are not in the room, and right now, AI is reshaping how that conversation gets shaped at scale.

McKinsey recently explored how agentic AI is restructuring the way marketing workflows operate, not just speeding them up, but fundamentally changing who makes decisions and when. For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this creates a specific challenge.

Here is what that actually means for you:

First, your brand identity has to be airtight before you automate anything. Garbage in, garbage out applies to AI just as much as it does to people.

Second, speed without strategy will amplify the wrong message faster than ever before.

Third, the companies winning at this stage are not chasing every new tool. They are defining what they stand for first, then deciding what to automate.

The question is not whether AI will touch your marketing. It already has. The question is: does your brand have a strong enough foundation to survive it?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey on agentic AI in marketing workflows caught our attention, and it should catch yours too.

The core argument is that AI is not just automating tasks anymore. It is making sequential decisions across entire marketing processes with minimal human intervention.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is a double-edged opportunity. The efficiency gains are real. But so is the risk of scaling a brand that has not yet defined its voice, its positioning, or its customer promise clearly enough.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams at this exact inflection point. The ones who scale well are not the ones who adopt AI fastest. They are the ones who know what their brand stands for before they hand over the wheel.

Read the McKinsey piece and ask yourself: is our brand ready to be automated?

AI is changing marketing faster than most leadership teams can track. But here is what does not change: whether your brand actually means something to the people you are trying to reach.

Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled What Does Your Marketing Smell Like, tackles this head on. Written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, the chapter challenges growing companies to think about brand in a way most executives have never considered.

The central idea is provocative on purpose. A strong brand is sensory. It is felt before it is understood. And when you are scaling from $50M toward $500M, that feeling either compounds your growth or quietly works against it.

Before you automate your marketing, you need to know what your brand actually stands for. That is where this chapter starts.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

SHRM recently reported that the new standard for hiring in 2026 is precision over scale. Companies chasing headcount without intent are building bloated teams that slow decisions, dilute culture, and punish the bottom line.

Here is what mid-market leaders scaling past $50M need to hear:

1. Every open role should map to a specific revenue or operational outcome. If you cannot name it, do not post the job.

2. Speed of hire is not a virtue if you are moving fast toward the wrong person. Quality of fit compounds over time. Mistakes compound faster.

3. Your talent strategy should be rebuilt annually. The skills that got you to $100M will not get you to $300M.

Most leadership teams treat hiring as a reaction to pressure. The ones who scale well treat it as a forward-looking investment with defined criteria and real accountability.

What does your current hiring process actually optimize for?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM makes a sharp argument: the era of high-volume, spray-and-pray hiring is over. In 2026, the companies winning on talent are the ones hiring with precision, not speed.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M. The leaders who build strong talent engines are not posting more jobs. They are getting ruthlessly clear on what a great hire actually looks like for their specific stage of growth, and then building a process that filters for exactly that.

Volume hiring might feel productive. It rarely is. Precision hiring feels slower up front and saves you enormous pain on the back end.

If your talent acquisition process has not been rebuilt since you crossed $50M in revenue, it is overdue. Read the full SHRM piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post3.text:

In Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond, Chapter 6, The Talent Engine, co-authored by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, tackles the core question that trips up nearly every scaling company: are you building a team for where you are, or for where you are going?

One of the insights that stops leaders in their tracks is this: your talent infrastructure breaks before your revenue does. Most founders do not see it coming because the warning signs look like growth.

Knowing what to look for and when to act is the difference between scaling and stalling.

post1.text:
More metrics will not save your business. They will bury it.

Leaders at the $50M+ level often believe that tracking more means knowing more. It does not. It means your team spends more time reporting than executing. Business.com recently catalogued 14 tools companies use to track KPIs, and the variety alone tells you something: most organizations are drowning in dashboards, not clarity.

Here is what high-performing scaling companies do differently:

1. They pick fewer than 10 metrics that directly connect to their strategic priorities. Not departmental vanity numbers. Not legacy reports no one acts on.

2. They assign a single owner to each metric. Shared accountability is no accountability.

3. They review metrics in the context of decisions, not rituals. If a weekly review never changes what anyone does on Monday, it is theater.

The companies that scale past $500M are not better at measuring everything. They are ruthless about measuring the right things.

What is the one metric your leadership team reviews every week that, honestly, nobody acts on?

post2.text:
A recent piece in the Hootsuite Blog lays out 31 social media KPIs worth tracking in 2026. It is a thorough list. That is also the problem.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, the instinct to track everything is understandable. But it creates a trap. When every metric matters, none of them do. Your team optimizes for the dashboard instead of the outcome.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders to cut through the noise and identify which numbers actually drive growth decisions. Social, operational, financial: the discipline is the same. Fewer metrics, sharper ownership, faster action.

If your reporting is growing faster than your revenue, that is a signal worth taking seriously.

Read the Hootsuite piece and ask yourself how many of those 31 you would actually act on: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiWEFVX3lxTE92dGhtdnRxbFlLRWJYQTVZWVNwcmdlUkVINjYtN1VqRkpqa2FUVXJYYjlubHdUcEtlSEplcnZXOWlMbWRqTE1tU0NGaWZMX1ZQYlRxeUQtb3k

post3.text:
Every scaling company eventually hits the same wall. The metrics multiply. The meetings multiply. The clarity disappears.

Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, 'Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond,' tackles this head-on. The chapter is called 'Death by KPIs,' and it was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, three leaders who have lived this problem inside real companies.

One thing they make clear: the issue is rarely a lack of data. It is a lack of discipline around which data earns a seat at the leadership table. They share a framework for identifying the metrics that actually move your business forward and eliminating the ones that just create noise.

If your team is tracking dozens of KPIs and still feels like it is flying blind, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling companies do not have a data problem. They have a discipline problem. By the time a business hits $50M, it has accumulated layers of reports, dashboards, and weekly reviews that consume leadership time without driving leadership decisions. The companies that break through to $500M and beyond share one habit: they ruthlessly cut the metrics that feel important from the ones that actually are.

post1.text:
Most companies are failing at AI not because the technology is bad, but because leadership is lying to themselves about how well it is working.

Research from NBER on global business AI adoption confirms what we see on the ground with scaling companies: deployment is happening, but productive use is lagging far behind. There is a gap between what executives report and what is actually showing up in output, revenue, or efficiency.

Here is what leaders at $50M and beyond need to hear:

1. AI adoption is not the same as AI integration. Installing tools is easy. Changing how your teams actually work is the hard part.

2. The productivity case for AI is not automatic. It has to be designed, measured, and managed like any other operational initiative.

3. If your employees are not bought in, your AI rollout is theater. Culture eats technology strategy for breakfast.

The companies that will win are not the ones moving fastest. They are the ones moving most intentionally.

Is your leadership team measuring AI by activity or by outcomes?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune reported something worth sitting with: 90% of executives say AI has not meaningfully improved productivity, yet many are still using it as justification to cut headcount.

That is a dangerous combination for any scaling company.

At Autobahn, we work with businesses in the $50M to $500M range. The ones getting burned by AI right now share one trait: they treated it as a cost-cutting tool before they understood it as a capability-building one. You cannot automate your way to scale if you have not first defined what excellent performance looks like in each function.

Before you reduce your team, ask whether AI has actually made your remaining team better. If the answer is unclear, you have an implementation problem, not a headcount problem.

Read the full Fortune article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifEFVX3lxTE5LZWF5Vkc3Wk9DVVd5aE83ZGVhbWMyb3U3MW1kcHljOHdwcjdjTmt1SmU5bFVRblVaZGJsRndNRS1fWExxc3IyZDBJcnlxZHhYVUFhV1pBSzVRS0R1RVJlNVYxM0pzRXZKcG96RExTdTVlMnhBWDNMUlVuUGM?oc=5

post3.text:
The New York Times recently highlighted a troubling disconnect: CEOs believe their AI rollouts are succeeding, while employees tell a very different story.

This gap is exactly what Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain tackle in Chapter 8 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

The chapter is built around something they call The Third Monitor Theory. It reframes how leaders at scaling companies should think about where AI actually fits in day-to-day work, and why most implementations fail before they ever get traction.

The insight is not about which tools to buy. It is about how humans and AI have to be positioned relative to each other for real productivity to follow.

If your team is running AI pilots that feel busy but are not moving numbers, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail their companies are often the ones who look the most confident in the room.

A leading psychologist recently flagged two traits we commonly celebrate in executives as actual warning signs. That should stop every growth-stage CEO cold.

Here is what scaling from $50M toward $500M actually requires you to reckon with:

1. Imposter syndrome is not a weakness to fix. At the $50M+ level, it is often a signal that you are finally operating at the edge of your genuine competence. That discomfort is data, not dysfunction.

2. Leaders who never question themselves are the dangerous ones. The executive who feels certain about everything stops learning exactly when the business needs adaptation most.

3. The goal is not confidence without doubt. It is the ability to act decisively while holding real uncertainty. Those are entirely different skills.

The leaders quietly doing the work of self-examination tend to build the most durable organizations.

So here is the question worth sitting with: Is your confidence serving your company, or protecting your ego?

#Leadership #ScalingUp #ExecutiveDevelopment

post2.text:
A recent piece in Psychology Today on quiet, introverted CEOs makes a point that most leadership development programs still refuse to accept: reserved leaders often outperform their louder counterparts, particularly during complex growth phases.

For companies scaling past $50M, this matters enormously. The pressure to perform authority, to project certainty, to dominate a boardroom, can actually push otherwise effective executives into behaviors that slow the organization down.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who are navigating exactly this tension. The ones who stop performing confidence and start building honest self-awareness tend to scale their teams and their revenues far more effectively.

If you lead or advise a growth-stage company, this article is worth your time.

post3.text:
Psychology Today recently explored what happens when confidence becomes a trap, when the very certainty that helped a leader succeed starts working against them.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business goes directly into that territory. Titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?", the chapter authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo takes on imposter syndrome not as a personal failing but as a predictable feature of scaling leadership.

One idea they surface that tends to land hard with growth-stage executives: the feeling that you do not belong at the next level is not proof that you should not be there. It may be proof that you are paying attention.

There is a framework in this chapter that changes how leaders read their own doubt. We will leave it there for now.

post1.text:
The most dangerous thing a scaling CEO can do is treat rest as a reward for performance.

It is not. Rest is a precondition for it.

The World Health Organization has been clear: poor mental health at work does not just affect individuals. It degrades organizational output at every level. For leaders running $50M to $500M operations, the cost is not abstract. It shows up in bad decisions, high turnover, and strategies that never get properly executed.

Here is what leaders at this stage get wrong about work-life design:

First, they confuse busyness with leverage. Logging 70-hour weeks feels productive until you realize you are the bottleneck in your own company.

Second, they build life around work instead of building work around life. At scale, that model breaks the leader before the business.

Third, they wait for a crisis to course-correct. By then, the cost is already paid.

The best-run companies at this revenue range are led by people who treat their own sustainability as a strategic asset.

When did you last design your life on purpose?

post2.text:
A recent piece in MIT Sloan Management Review makes a compelling case that burnout is not a personal failure. It is an organizational design problem.

That distinction matters enormously for companies scaling through the $50M to $500M range.

At that stage, growth pressure is relentless. Leaders assume the solution is hiring more people or pushing harder. But if the structure of work itself is producing exhaustion, more headcount just spreads the problem further.

At Autobahn, we see this consistently. The companies that scale well are the ones that deliberately design how work gets done, not just how much of it gets done.

If your team is burning out, the question is not who needs to toughen up. The question is what in your operating model needs to change.

Read the full piece here and think about what it means for your organization: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMidkFVX3lxTE9PT0FJeXRxYlBWcHY5bkt3TkNoclFfTmhSWUFDTld1alFEVEcxR1Fvc0hDbGxERm0tbGR3aDVtWkhURHZRb1Fwak1KMnAtMUM3MFdINDkyRWlHOGdRdHJjNldhTjVoR3dDUEJtTUN2akFfaGhqNnc

post3.text:
The American Psychological Association has been sounding the alarm on workplace burnout for years. Employers are still not listening at the rate the problem demands.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head-on. The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, and it was written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain.

The core premise is one that most scaling leaders resist: sustainable growth requires deliberate life planning, not just business planning. The two are not separate conversations.

Samantha brings a framework into this chapter that helps leaders at the $50M-plus stage think about how they want to live, not just how they want to perform. The insight that tends to land hardest is about what you are actually optimizing for when you say yes to everything.

We will leave that one for the book.
